B4C1: Introduces Book Four's plan: after truths about God knowable by reason, Aquinas turns to truths above reason revealed by faith — the Trinity, the Incarnation, the sacraments, and man's final resurrection and glory.
B4C2: Establishes from Scripture that God the Father truly and eternally begets a Son, Jesus Christ, introducing divine generation, paternity, and filiation as the starting point for treating the Trinity.
B4C3: Argues from Scriptural texts, especially John's Prologue, that the Son begotten of the Father is truly God himself, not merely a creature called "son" in a figurative or adoptive sense.
B4C4: States and refutes Photinus's view that Christ was a mere man who became "Son of God" only by merit, showing Scripture teaches a true, eternal, natural divine sonship.
B4C5: States and refutes Sabellius's view that Father and Son are one Person under different names, the title "Son" assumed only at Christ's birth, showing Scripture distinguishes real, eternal Persons.
B4C6: Marshals Scriptural texts that seem to suggest Christ was exalted, named, or made divine only in time — e.g. "God hath made him Lord and Christ" — posing objections later chapters will resolve.
B4C7: Refutes Arius's claim that the Son is merely an exalted creature inferior to the Father, showing Scripture ascribes to the Son a true, equal divinity distinct from that of angels or adopted sons.
B4C8: Answers the Scriptural texts Arians cite in their own favor, showing that Father and Son share one identical divine essence and nature, and so are not two Gods but one.
B4C9: Explains disputed texts quoted by Photinus and Sabellius (such as "all power is given to me") in ways consistent with Christ's eternal divine sonship, refuting both errors.
B4C10: Lists rational difficulties human reason meets in the mystery of divine generation and procession, given that generation ordinarily implies change, which cannot occur in the unchangeable, simple God.
B4C11: Explains divine generation by analogy to intellectual emanation — as a mind conceives an inner word — showing how the Son proceeds from the Father without change, division, or matter.
B4C12: Shows how the Son, as the Word conceived through the Father's self-understanding, is rightly called the Wisdom of God, just as an act can take the name of the habit producing it.
B4C13: Argues that since God understands himself and all things in a single simple act, only one Word is conceived, and therefore only one Son is begotten of the Father.
B4C14: Resolves the rational difficulties raised earlier by showing that intellectual generation, unlike material generation, involves no change, corruption, or succession in the unchangeable God.
B4C15: Shows from Scripture that beside the Father and Son, a third Person, the Holy Ghost, is numbered in God and proceeds distinctly, especially from the Father through the Son.
B4C16: Presents Scriptural texts some have misused to argue that the Holy Ghost is merely a superior creature formed by God rather than truly divine.
B4C17: Proves from Scripture — for instance, that believers are called "temples of the Holy Ghost" — that the Holy Ghost is truly God and not a creature.
B4C18: Refutes views that the Holy Ghost is merely the shared Godhead of Father and Son, or an accidental gift like wisdom, showing he is a real subsistent Person who acts by will.
B4C19: Using the analogy of intellect and will, explains how the Holy Ghost proceeds as subsistent Love, distinct in Person from Father and Son yet one with them in essence.
B4C20: Explains how Scripture attributes creation and providence over all things to divine Love — the Holy Ghost — since God's love of his own goodness is the cause of created things existing.
B4C21: Explains how the Holy Ghost, as subsistent Love, is specially "given" to rational creatures insofar as grace makes them like divine love through the gift of charity.
B4C22: Describes how the Holy Ghost draws souls into friendship and contemplative union with God, producing love, joy, peace, and the other spiritual gifts named by the Apostle.
B4C23: Answers the earlier objections by explaining Scripture's varied senses of the word "spirit," showing none of the disputed texts imply the Holy Ghost is a mere creature.
B4C24: Argues from Scripture, which calls the Holy Ghost the "Spirit of the Son," that the Holy Ghost proceeds from the Son as well as from the Father.
B4C25: States and dismisses the objection that, since Christ spoke of the Spirit proceeding only "from the Father," the Son cannot also be a principle of that procession.
B4C26: Concludes that only three Persons — Father, Son, and Holy Ghost — subsist in the one divine nature, distinguished solely by their relations of origin, with no fourth possible.
B4C27: Opens the treatment of the Incarnation, calling it the most wondrous of God's works, and surveys what Scripture teaches about the eternal Word becoming flesh.
B4C28: Refutes the view, held by Photinus and others, that Christ was a mere man who earned divine status by his deeds, showing this would empty the Incarnation of real meaning.
B4C29: Refutes the Manichean claim that Christ's body was only apparent or imaginary, showing this reduces his birth, suffering, and death to mere fiction, contrary to Scripture.
B4C30: Refutes Valentine's teaching that Christ brought a heavenly body through Mary without truly deriving flesh from her, showing this denies Christ's true, complete human nature.
B4C31: Refutes Apollinaris's claim that Christ's flesh was formed by transformation of the Word itself, rather than assumed from the Virgin's own substance.
B4C32: Refutes Arius's claim that Christ had no human soul, the Godhead itself supplying its place, showing this denies Christ's true and complete humanity.
B4C33: Refutes Apollinaris's claim that Christ's soul lacked mind and reason, and Origen's claim that Christ's soul was created and pre-existed before the world.
B4C34: Refutes Theodore of Mopsuestia and Nestorius, who taught that the Word and the man Christ were joined only loosely, as by moral indwelling, rather than in one Person.
B4C35: Refutes Eutyches's claim that Christ's divine and human natures merged into a single composite nature, defending one Person subsisting in two distinct, unconfused natures.
B4C36: Refutes the Monothelite view of Macarius of Antioch that Christ had only one will and operation, arguing two complete natures entail two distinct wills and modes of acting.
B4C37: Refutes theologians who, to avoid granting the Word a complete human hypostasis, held that Christ's body and soul were not truly united as in ordinary human beings.
B4C38: Refutes the view that a complete human person, distinct from the Word, was joined to God only personally, effectively producing two supposits under a shared "person."
B4C39: States the orthodox Catholic doctrine: one divine Person with two complete, unconfused natures united in a single hypostasis, the standard by which all the prior errors are judged.
B4C40: Lists the philosophical objections unbelievers raise against the very possibility of God becoming man, to be answered systematically in the chapters that follow.
B4C41: Clarifies the technical sense in which God and man were united "in the person, not in the nature," distinguishing the several meanings the word "nature" can bear.
B4C42: Argues it was especially fitting that the Word, rather than the Father or the Holy Ghost, assumed human nature, given the Word's natural affinity to reason and understanding.
B4C43: Argues the human nature united to the Word began to exist only in and through that very union, at the moment of Christ's conception, rather than pre-existing separately.
B4C44: Argues that Christ's body was informed by a complete rational soul from the very instant of its conception, rather than developing gradually as in ordinary human generation.
B4C45: Argues that since Christ's body was instantly and fully formed, ordinary male seed — which shapes a body only over time — could not be its active principle, hence the virgin birth.
B4C46: Explains why the fashioning of Christ's body, though a common work of the whole Trinity, is fittingly appropriated to the Holy Ghost, in parallel with the Word's own eternal generation.
B4C47: Clarifies that though Christ was conceived by the Holy Ghost's power, the Spirit is not thereby his "father," since he acted as efficient cause rather than contributing his own substance.
B4C48: Argues that although Christ's human nature is a creature, the single Person of Christ, subsisting also in the uncreated Godhead, cannot without qualification be called simply "a creature."
B4C49: Answers the philosophical objections to the Incarnation raised earlier, clarifying that the Word underwent no change or composition in becoming man; only the assumed human nature came to be.
B4C50: Argues, against the Pelagians, that Adam's sin is truly transmitted to and inherited by all his descendants, establishing humanity's need for the remedy of the Incarnation.
B4C51: Presents rational objections to the doctrine of inherited original sin, notably that guilt cannot justly be imputed to descendants for what lay outside their own free choice.
B4C52: Answers the objections of the previous chapter, explaining how the whole human race, as one body derived from Adam, can justly share the disorder and penalty of his sin.
B4C53: Presents objections claiming it is beneath divine dignity and contrary to the order of the universe for God to unite himself personally to lowly human nature.
B4C54: Shows the profound fittingness and wisdom of the Incarnation, especially as it perfects man's hope, knowledge, and love of God on the road to eternal happiness.
B4C55: Answers the objections against the fittingness of the Incarnation, showing it does not disturb cosmic order since man, through his intellect, is naturally ordered toward union with God.
B4C56: Explains why Christ's saving power, though a universal cause of salvation, needed to be applied to individuals through visible sacramental signs suited to man's sense-based nature.
B4C57: Explains that sacraments of the Old Law only signified and promised the salvation to come, while sacraments of the New Law actually confer the grace won by Christ's Passion.
B4C58: Derives the sevenfold number of the sacraments of the New Law by analogy with the stages and needs of bodily life — birth, growth, nourishment, healing, and propagation.
B4C59: Explains Baptism as spiritual regeneration that removes both original and actual sin, conferring new spiritual life symbolized fittingly by the cleansing action of water.
B4C60: Explains Confirmation as the sacrament perfecting spiritual strength, arming the baptized as a soldier of Christ able to confess the faith fearlessly before others.
B4C61: Explains the Eucharist as spiritual nourishment that sustains and increases the soul's life, given under the forms of bread and wine, mankind's ordinary food.
B4C62: States the view of heretics who hold that Christ's body and blood are present in the Eucharist only symbolically or in signification, not in true reality, preparing to refute it.
B4C63: Explains that Christ becomes present in the Eucharist not by local movement but by the whole substance of bread being converted into his body — transubstantiation.
B4C64: Explains how Christ's body, present through transubstantiation, occupies the place defined by the bread's remaining dimensions, with other realities present by natural concomitance.
B4C65: Explains how the accidents of bread and wine — taste, appearance, and the rest — remain without their natural substance after consecration, sustained instead by quantity alone.
B4C66: Explains how the sensible accidents of bread and wine, though lacking their natural subject, can still act on the senses and undergo change exactly as before consecration.
B4C67: Explains that breaking the host affects only the persisting dimensive quantity, not Christ's substance, which remains whole and entire and undivided in every resulting part.
B4C68: Clarifies Christ's words "the words I have spoken are spirit and life," showing they mean his flesh is received spiritually, not that his real sacramental presence is denied.
B4C69: Specifies that valid Eucharistic matter requires true wheaten bread and grape wine, and that substitutes or heavy admixtures which destroy their proper species cannot be used.
B4C70: Explains that sacramental grace, received into the soul as a habit, does not remove the will's freedom, so a person can still choose to sin even after receiving it.
B4C71: Argues that just as one can fall from grace by sinning, the wayfaring will remains changeable in the other direction too, so a sinner can be restored to grace by repentance.
B4C72: Explains Penance as the sacramental remedy — a spiritual healing rather than a rebirth — by which sins committed after Baptism are forgiven through contrition, confession, and satisfaction.
B4C73: Explains Extreme Unction as a sacrament addressing the lingering effects of sin that weaken the soul through bodily infirmity, administered as spiritual healing near death.
B4C74: Explains that since sacraments must be dispensed by visible human ministers endowed with spiritual power, Christ instituted Holy Order to confer this ministerial authority.
B4C75: Explains, by analogy with subordinate arts serving one ultimate end, the graded hierarchy of orders within the priesthood, each subserving the highest sacramental purpose.
B4C76: Explains the episcopal office as a power surpassing that of ordinary priests in governing the faithful, and argues that one supreme bishop presides over the whole Church.
B4C77: Argues that the sacramental power conferred at ordination remains permanently in the minister, so valid sacraments can still be administered even by sinful or unworthy clergy.
B4C78: Explains Matrimony as instituted to serve the several ends of human generation — propagation of the species, the good of offspring, and social order — and its sacramental status in the New Law.
B4C79: Argues that since Christ delivered mankind from both sin and death, its punishment, his own bodily resurrection guarantees and causes the future resurrection of all human bodies.
B4C80: Presents philosophical difficulties raised against bodily resurrection, notably that a thing once destroyed and dissolved cannot naturally return as numerically the same identical individual.
B4C81: Resolves the objections against resurrection by explaining that the incorruptibility man's body originally possessed and lost through sin can be restored by God's power to the same body.
B4C82: Argues that since Christ's merit is more powerful to restore life than Adam's sin was to cause death, those who rise again through Christ will never die a second time.
B4C83: Argues that since food and sexual union exist only to preserve corruptible mortal life, the immortal risen body will have no need or use for either after resurrection.
B4C84: Refutes opinions that risen bodies will be purely spiritual or rarefied like air, defending that they will be true composite bodies made of the same elements as before.
B4C85: Explains that although of the same nature as now, risen bodies of both the good and the wicked will be incorruptible, fitted to receive an everlasting reward or punishment.
B4C86: Explains that the bodies of the blessed will receive from the glorified soul special gifts — impassibility, subtlety, agility, and clarity — befitting the soul's beatitude.
B4C87: Argues that glorified bodies, sharing properties of the heavenly bodies, will dwell above the heavens together with Christ rather than remain confined to earth's lowest region.
B4C88: Argues that the risen will retain their own sex, since it belongs to the integrity of human nature, and will rise again at a perfect age, neither infant nor decrepit.
B4C89: Explains that the damned will rise incorruptible and complete in body, since this belongs to nature, yet without the added gifts of glory, so as to suffer fittingly forever.
B4C90: Explains that demons and the souls of the damned can be tormented by material fire not through physical alteration of their nature but by being bound to or confined by it.
B4C91: Argues that since the separated soul is immediately capable of the beatific vision or of suffering, there is no reason for God to delay its reward or punishment until the resurrection.
B4C92: Argues that once separated from the body, the souls of the just, no longer in a state of trial, become permanently unable to turn their will away from the good.
B4C93: Argues that the souls of the damned likewise become permanently fixed in their disordered will after death, since their punishment would not be truly everlasting if their will could still change.
B4C94: Extends the same unchangeable fixity of will to souls who die in charity but still need cleansing, showing that they too cannot alter their ultimate orientation toward God.
B4C95: Explains that the will's fixity after death in every case traces to the soul's settled relation to its final end, comparable to the unchangeableness of the intellect's first principles.
B4C96: Explains that a twofold judgment corresponds to a twofold reward: one given to each soul individually immediately at death, and another given to all together, body and soul, at the general resurrection.
B4C97: Describes how, once human nature reaches its final incorruptible state after judgment, the whole corporeal universe will likewise be transformed and freed from generation and corruption to suit man's glorified condition.
